questions.q: In his experiment with the cathode ray tube, what quantity did J.J. Thomson succeed in measuring for the cathode ray particles, later called electrons?
options: The charge-to-mass ratio of the cathode ray particles
The charge of a single particle on its own
The mass of a single particle on its own
Only the velocity of the particles
questions.explanation: Thomson built a cathode ray tube with charged parallel plates and a magnetic field and succeeded in measuring the charge-to-mass ratio of the particles. Every force he could apply depended on both charge and mass together, so he could extract only their ratio, not the charge or the mass alone.

questions.q: Thomson's experiment involved two stages. In the first stage the magnetic and electric fields' opposing forces were varied until they cancelled, leaving the cathode rays undeflected. What did this first stage determine?
options: The velocity of the cathode-ray particles
The charge on each cathode-ray particle
The radius of the circular path
The mass of each cathode-ray particle
questions.explanation: With both fields on and their opposing forces cancelling, the beam passes through undeflected. Equating the electric and magnetic force equations lets the charge cancel, giving the velocity (v = E/B). The second stage then uses the magnetic field alone, bending the beam into a circle whose radius yields the charge-to-mass ratio.

questions.q: Outline how, by adjusting the strengths of the electric and magnetic fields, a charged particle can be made to travel along a straight, undeflected path through crossed fields.
keyPoints: The electric field, the magnetic field and the velocity of the particle are arranged at right angles to each other.
By adjusting the strengths of the electric and magnetic fields, the two forces on the particle directly oppose each other.
When the opposing forces cancel, the net force is zero and the particle travels along a straight path (undeflected) — this is the velocity selector.
questions.explanation: If you recalled the mutually-perpendicular geometry and that adjusting the field strengths makes the electric and magnetic forces cancel so the particle goes straight through, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: An electron of charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C moves at 2.5 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a magnetic field of strength 2.0 × 10⁻² T. Calculate the magnetic force on the electron, and state the shape of the path it follows.
working: The path is circular, because the magnetic force always acts perpendicular to the velocity of the electron.
questions.explanation: Direct use of F = qvB sinθ with θ = 90° (so sinθ = 1). Because the force stays perpendicular to the velocity it does no work, the speed is unchanged, and the path is a circle, not a parabola.

questions.q: In Millikan's oil drop experiment an oil drop of mass 6.8 × 10⁻⁶ g is suspended between two parallel plates separated by 3.5 mm with 110 V across them. The weight force balances the electric force (F_g = F_E). Calculate the charge on the oil drop. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
working: For suspension \(F_g = F_E\), so \(mg = Eq\) and \(q = \dfrac{mg}{E}\)
questions.explanation: Suspended means the upward electric force balances the downward weight, so q = mg/E. Watch the grams-to-kilograms conversion (6.8 × 10⁻⁶ g = 6.8 × 10⁻⁹ kg) — a classic slip.

questions.q: Millikan's oil drop experiment showed that the charge on an oil drop always occurred in 'packets' or multiples of one smallest value. What is this value, the elementary charge found on an electron?
questions.explanation: Millikan measured drop after drop and found the charge was never arbitrary: it always came in whole-number multiples of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the elementary charge. This showed that electric charge is quantised. He won the Nobel Prize for this in 1923.

questions.q: According to Thomson's plum pudding model, how is the structure of the atom described?
options: A positively charged fluid with negatively charged electrons scattered throughout it
A tiny dense positive nucleus orbited by electrons at a distance
Electrons fixed in discrete energy levels around an empty centre
A neutral cloud of matter waves with no internal charge
questions.explanation: Having found the electron, Thomson proposed the atom must consist of a positively charged fluid with his negatively charged electrons scattered throughout it — like plums in a plum pudding. The concentrated nucleus came later, from Rutherford's gold foil experiment.

questions.q: Distinguish correctly between what Thomson's experiment and Millikan's experiment each determined.
options: Thomson found the charge-to-mass ratio; Millikan found the elementary charge
Thomson found the elementary charge; Millikan found the charge-to-mass ratio
Both found the mass of the electron independently
Thomson found the mass; Millikan found the charge-to-mass ratio
questions.explanation: Thomson measured the charge-to-mass ratio (about 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹) but not the charge or mass separately. Millikan measured the elementary charge by itself. Memory hook: Thomson gives The ratio, Millikan gives the Magnitude of the charge. Only combining the two yields the electron's mass.

questions.q: A beam of cathode rays passes undeflected through crossed fields when the electric field is 5.0 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and the magnetic field is 2.0 × 10⁻² T. Calculate the speed of the particles.
working: Undeflected means the electric force balances the magnetic force: \(qE = qvB\)
The charge \(q\) cancels from both sides: \(v = \dfrac{E}{B}\)
questions.explanation: The balance condition qE = qvB lets the charge cancel, giving v = E/B. Because the charge (and mass) cancel out, this selected speed is independent of the particle's charge and mass — the defining feature of a velocity selector.

questions.q: Evaluate the evidence supporting the plum pudding model of the atom. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The plum pudding model proposed a sphere of diffuse positive charge with the negative electrons embedded throughout it. The evidence supported it in several ways: it incorporated Thomson's newly discovered electrons; the diffuse positive charge balanced the electrons, correctly making the atom electrically neutral overall; and it was consistent with the new evidence that atoms are divisible. However, its central claim — the distribution of the positive charge — had no direct experimental support; the positive 'pudding' was assumed rather than tested. Therefore the model was a reasonable interpretation of the evidence available at the time, but its untested positive distribution is precisely what the Geiger–Marsden gold foil experiment later disproved by revealing a concentrated nucleus.

criteria.descriptor: States strengths: incorporates electrons and/or makes the atom electrically neutral.
Notes consistency with atoms being divisible (having internal parts).
Identifies the limitation: the diffuse positive distribution was assumed, not tested.
Reaches a judgement with explicit contrast (e.g. 'but'), linking to its later overturning by the gold foil experiment.

questions.explanation: An 'evaluate' demands balance: strengths, then limitation, then a judgement. The pivot word 'but' flags the contrast and earns the top marks.

questions.q: From memory: how are Thomson's and Millikan's results combined to obtain the mass of the electron, and what is its approximate value?
keyPoints: Thomson gives the charge-to-mass ratio (q/m ≈ 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹); Millikan gives the charge (q ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
Dividing the charge by the charge-to-mass ratio cancels the charge, leaving the mass: m = q / (q/m).
This gives the electron mass ≈ 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg — neither experiment alone could give it.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that you divide Millikan's charge by Thomson's ratio to cancel the charge and land on about 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, grade yourself Good or Easy.
